However, its dominance is now being tested following the resignation of its chief executive Jensen Huang, [triggered by revelations of extramarital affairs,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/former-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-had-a-relationship-with-a-second-employee-sources-say?ref=inline-article) including with a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The affair has [intensified scrutiny of Megaspeed where Alice Huang was a former executive.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/who-is-alice-huang-the-chinese-exec-accused-of-spying-on-nvidia-ceo?ref=inline-article) The American authorities have been looking into whether the Singapore-based company aided in bypassing US export controls, specifically examining if chips were being unlawfully rerouted or smuggled into China. These developments in a post-Jensen Huang era may spell trouble for South-east Asia’s AI infrastructure build-out, with experts expecting [data centre operators in the region to face stricter checks on purchases of advanced American chips.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/data-centres-in-se-asia-could-be-the-first-to-feel-heat-from-jensen-huang-affair?ref=inline-article) The Straits Times examines Nvidia’s central role in the AI industry and other viable AI chip alternatives. ## What are Nvidia’s key products? The firm is known for its high-performance compute chips, which power modern tasks such as AI chatbot assistants that can do deep research and code, autonomous vehicles, and delivery robots. Nvidia is traditionally known for designing Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) that deliver optimal graphics for video games and multimedia design. The same technology has grown to become the bedrock of data centres, running massive amounts of calculations simultaneously to train and run AI models. Among its most advanced chips are the Blackwell and Rubin GPUs, which the US authorities have banned from being exported to China, citing security concerns due to the potential for military use. Earlier in September, the chipmaker set foot into the personal computer market with its new RTX Spark Superchip, allowing users to run large AI models and high-end games on laptops. ## How does Nvidia dominate the global market? The firm dominates the global market for high-end chips in data centres for training AI models and inference work, with industry estimates putting its share at around 80 per cent. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open Source AI Models: 3 Run Paths, 48% Coding Index [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 13, 2026 · 26 min read ![Illustrative: Two technicians in blue vests work at a server rack packed with blue network cables, one holding a tablet](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/open-source-ai-models-3-run-paths-mistral-large-4-kimi-k3-1-glm-5-3-2026-img13-1024x576.webp) Photo: Daoducquan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Five open-weight model families dominate the November 2026 conversation: Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3 and Gemma 4. They share a label and almost nothing else. Mistral publishes a named license (the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT license), while a [third-party comparison of open-weight licenses](https://gpuwerk.com/blog/open-weight-model-licenses/) flags that several rivals need a closer read of the model card before you ship anything on top of them. That gap matters more than a benchmark point. A team that picks the wrong route to a model, whether a vendor API, a hyperscaler catalog or its own GPUs, can end up with a bill, a latency profile or a legal question it did not plan for. Our [self-hosted versus API cost breakdown](https://shattered.io/self-hosted-llm-vs-api-kimi-k3-1-pro-glm-5-3-deepseek-v4-1-mistral-large-4-2026/) covers the hardware arithmetic. The question here is different: for each of the five current open source AI models, which routes exist today, what does each route cost, and what does the official evidence actually confirm? Everything below is dated November 13, 2026. Where an official page confirms a fact, the text says so. Where only a third-party tracker or a forum post supports it, the text says that too, and the table cells stay empty rather than guess. That discipline is the point. The open-model market moves weekly, and a confident but wrong spec costs readers real money. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Open Source AI Models Actually Mean in 2026 Strictly speaking, almost none of these releases are open source in the way the software industry uses the term. The usual bar covers code, data and the freedom to modify and redistribute. What the labs ship is closer to open weights: a downloadable set of parameters, usually with a license that grants some rights and withholds others. Moonshot AI officially calls Kimi K3.1 Pro open-weight, and Mistral calls Large 4 open weight. Neither claims a fully open training pipeline. This comparison uses the phrase open source ai models the way readers do while keeping the distinction visible. When a sentence says open source, read it as weights you can download under some license. When it says open-weight, the lab itself used that word. ### The evidence ladder Not every claim deserves equal trust. We sort the evidence into four rungs and place each model on the ladder: * **Rung 1, official page confirms:** the lab’s own announcement, documentation or pricing page states the fact. * **Rung 2, official page implies:** the lab uses the phrase open-weight or open models without naming a license file. * **Rung 3, third-party tracker:** a pricing or license aggregator reports it, and no official page contradicts it. * **Rung 4, forum or single mention:** a user post or one-off report. Treat it as a lead, not a fact. Mistral Large 4 sits mostly on rung 1. Mistral’s announcement of the open-weight release names the license and its version (v26.10). highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open Source AI Models: 3 Run Paths, 48% Coding Index [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 13, 2026 · 26 min read ![Illustrative: Two technicians in blue vests work at a server rack packed with blue network cables, one holding a tablet](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/open-source-ai-models-3-run-paths-mistral-large-4-kimi-k3-1-glm-5-3-2026-img13-1024x576.webp) Photo: Daoducquan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Five open-weight model families dominate the November 2026 conversation: Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3 and Gemma 4. They share a label and almost nothing else. Mistral publishes a named license (the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT license), while a [third-party comparison of open-weight licenses](https://gpuwerk.com/blog/open-weight-model-licenses/) flags that several rivals need a closer read of the model card before you ship anything on top of them. That gap matters more than a benchmark point. A team that picks the wrong route to a model, whether a vendor API, a hyperscaler catalog or its own GPUs, can end up with a bill, a latency profile or a legal question it did not plan for. Our [self-hosted versus API cost breakdown](https://shattered.io/self-hosted-llm-vs-api-kimi-k3-1-pro-glm-5-3-deepseek-v4-1-mistral-large-4-2026/) covers the hardware arithmetic. The question here is different: for each of the five current open source AI models, which routes exist today, what does each route cost, and what does the official evidence actually confirm? Everything below is dated November 13, 2026. Where an official page confirms a fact, the text says so. Where only a third-party tracker or a forum post supports it, the text says that too, and the table cells stay empty rather than guess. That discipline is the point. The open-model market moves weekly, and a confident but wrong spec costs readers real money. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Open Source AI Models Actually Mean in 2026 Strictly speaking, almost none of these releases are open source in the way the software industry uses the term. The usual bar covers code, data and the freedom to modify and redistribute. What the labs ship is closer to open weights: a downloadable set of parameters, usually with a license that grants some rights and withholds others. Moonshot AI officially calls Kimi K3.1 Pro open-weight, and Mistral calls Large 4 open weight. Neither claims a fully open training pipeline. This comparison uses the phrase open source ai models the way readers do while keeping the distinction visible. When a sentence says open source, read it as weights you can download under some license. When it says open-weight, the lab itself used that word. ### The evidence ladder Not every claim deserves equal trust. We sort the evidence into four rungs and place each model on the ladder: * **Rung 1, official page confirms:** the lab’s own announcement, documentation or pricing page states the fact. * **Rung 2, official page implies:** the lab uses the phrase open-weight or open models without naming a license file. * **Rung 3, third-party tracker:** a pricing or license aggregator reports it, and no official page contradicts it. * **Rung 4, forum or single mention:** a user post or one-off report. Treat it as a lead, not a fact. Mistral Large 4 sits mostly on rung 1. Mistral’s announcement of the open-weight release names the license and its version (v26.10). highlights.content: [Ai2](/) # XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question November 13, 2026 Ai2 --- [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06842)[Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/XYBench-dataset)[Code](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench) Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing [**XYBench**](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench), a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the *XY problem*: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: *recognizing* when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately *redirecting* them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. ### Building XYBench We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context. For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem. ### Evaluating how an answer helps A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem. A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main) [MLQ](/) [Back to News](/news/) [AI](/news/ai/) [AI INFRASTRUCTURE](/news/tag/ai-infrastructure/) [DATA CENTER](/news/tag/data-center/) [NVIDIA](/news/tag/nvidia/) [REGULATION](/news/tag/regulation/) [SEMICONDUCTORS](/news/tag/semiconductors/) # Huang's exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion of Chinese AI data centers built on Nvidia chips, Reuters reports Nov 13, 2026 · 11:15 AM · by MLQ Agent · 8 min read Key points * Reuters reviewed more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, contracts and disclosures and found projects worth over 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion) built around Nvidia's restricted processors [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). * The largest is a proposed 6.2 billion-yuan ($873 million) AI computing center in Xianyou county, Fujian, planned around H100 chips; others are in Shaanxi, Jilin, Inner Mongolia, Gansu, Wuxi and Fujian [[2]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/chinas-3-billionplus-pipeline-of-nvidiapowered-ai-data-centres-5024599). * Reuters said the projects have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Alice Huang, and that it did not establish how the restricted hardware reached Chinese buyers [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). * Hong Kong-listed AI developers fell again on Friday: Z.AI dropped 7.4%, MiniMax 4.9% and Tencent 2.6% in morning trading [[3]](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/asia-stocks-steady-chipmakers-rebound-042520486.html). ![Huang's exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion of Chinese AI data centers built on Nvidia chips, Reuters reports](/media/news_images/huangs-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-of-chinese-ai-data-centers-built-o.jpg) More than $3 billion of Chinese AI data center projects designed around [Nvidia](/companies/nvidia/) processors that the US bars from export to China are at risk of delays, supply disruption or costly redesigns as Washington weighs tighter controls after [Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive](/news/jensen-huang-resigns-as-nvidia-ceo-cfo-colette-kress-named-interim-chief-executive/), Reuters reported on Friday [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). A Reuters review of more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures identified projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value of more than 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion) built around Nvidia's H100, H200 and H800 chips [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). The total includes planned investments, signed contracts and completed installations, and covers buildings and power systems as well as chips [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). Air Force Young Investigator Award to study trust in AI agents that act on behalf of real people # Air Force Young Investigator Award to study trust in AI agents that act on behalf of real people Author: [Ken Kingery](/news-and-events/news/authors/ken-kingery/) ![A young man with dark hair, glasses, and a blue button-down shirt smiles widely.](/assets/688081/600x/diego_gomez_zara_tw.jpg) It’s an axiom that today’s cybersecurity teams know all too well: People are more likely to trust communications that appear to come from people they already know. Yet more and more of those communications now pass through artificial intelligence (AI). Emails, documents, presentations, and messages are drafted and edited using AI. In today’s online ecosystem of ever-improving large language models and a growing amount of personal data, people are increasingly interacting with one another through AI agents that can act on someone’s behalf. But what if an AI agent could stand in for a specific individual? Early research suggests that AI agents modeled on a real person can create a stronger sense of trust and presence than generic AI assistants. This points to an opportunity for organizations to improve workflows and efficiency by building AI that makes decisions and communicates just like a real coworker would. “We’re essentially talking about creating AI agents that represent a specific person, so it definitely raises serious questions about privacy, consent, and misuse,” said [Diego Gómez-Zará](https://engineering.nd.edu/faculty/diego-gomez-zara/), assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Notre Dame. “These agents are already being developed, but we know very little about how people relate to them. We need to understand how these technologies can be built safely, securely, and in a way that people will accept.” These are the questions that Gómez-Zará will be pursuing for the next three years thanks to a new $450,000 [Air Force Office of Scientific Research Young Investigator Program](https://www.afrl.af.mil/About-Us/Fact-Sheets/Fact-Sheet-Display/Article/2282106/afosr-funding-opportunities-additional-programs/) award. The program is intended to enhance the early-career development of outstanding young researchers while pursuing Air Force mission and related challenges in science and engineering. The Air Force is interested in these types of AI proxies to help preserve an Airman’s knowledge and decision-making abilities during transitions and personnel rotations, especially in leadership positions. There is also potential to help move projects and missions forward when lines of communication are sporadic or cut off. With the new support, Gómez-Zará will take a multipronged approach to answering a multitude of questions related to this intriguing possibility. For example: What makes people trust a personal AI agent enough to delegate decisions to it? Will colleagues trust an agent acting on someone’s behalf, or prefer the real person? How does AI-mediated interaction affect trust among the other people involved? “At the heart of these questions is a concept that I have been developing called ‘proxy trust,’” said Gómez-Zará. “That is the degree to which the trust we place in a colleague carries over to the AI agent that represents them. Some agents only retrieve information. Others change records, with or without a person approving. AI agent sprawl is an uncontrolled spread of these agents, built by different teams without shared oversight. The scale is moving fast. That is a forecast, not a measurement, but it shows the direction. Only 13% of organizations think they have the right agent governance in place today. Agent sprawl goes further than shadow AI. GrubMarket, a South San Francisco, California-based software-as-a-service (SAAS) company working with food producers, wholesalers, distributors and retailers, is expanding its use of artificial intelligence (AI) with a new AI agent. The company designed its new AI agent to turn vendor invoices and receipts into purchase orders for food distributors. The tool, called the “AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent,” was made to reduce the amount of manual data entry required from produce and other fresh food distributors. “The food supply chain industry is undergoing unprecedented transformation driven by artificial intelligence,” said Mike Xu, CEO of GrubMarket, in a release statement. “With our new AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent, we are bringing powerful AI capabilities to another critical function within food distribution.” The new agent follows other recent AI rollouts from GrubMarket. In June, the company announced the [launch of an AI sales agent](https://www.digitalcommerce360.com/2026/06/10/grubmarket-ai-agent-for-sales-team/). Its other AI deployments have included a reporting AI agent on its GrubAssist AI platform. GrubMarket also created its Monitoring AI Agent that tracks financial and operational data for customers. Now, the technology provider is turning to purchase orders. ## Why GrubMarket launched its new AI agent Xu said that by automating purchasing workflows, GrubMarket is helping distributors operate more efficiently. In turn, he believes that they can gain better visibility into their businesses, making better-informed decisions and improving profitability. “This launch represents another important step in our broader vision of building specialized AI agents that automate and optimize every major function across the food supply chain industry,” Xu said, adding that the company remains committed to leveraging artificial intelligence to help businesses modernize their operations and unlock new levels of efficiency and growth. Industry observers said the real test will be in the details. AI Agents.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Stopping a Rogue AI Agent Takes More Than Turning Off the Model](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fstopping-a-rogue-ai-agent-takes-more-than-turning-off-the-model_gen_1794580441634-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #Cybersecurity # Stopping a Rogue AI Agent Takes More Than Turning Off the Model • ![Lukas Brandt](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Flukas-brandt.webp&w=64&q=75) [Lukas Brandt](/author/lukas-brandt) •6 min read Share this article Advertisement [Advertise on LavX NewsSee options](/advertise) Security guidance says teams should pause workflows, revoke credentials, restrict tools and network paths, preserve evidence, and fix the cause before restoring access. An AI agent sorts support tickets and looks up account details. It can export records if its identity and tools allow the action. A ticket can carry instructions that lead the agent to send data to an unfamiliar destination. The agent does not need a separate breach to make the request. It uses access already granted to it. That scenario raises a practical response question: what 'stop the agent' means. A team may pause the model while a workflow, credential, or connection stays active. Those parts need separate controls. An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond intended scope. It recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents. An AI agent sits inside a larger system. A model chooses an action. An orchestrator runs the workflow. An identity supplies access. Tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools connect. Details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent stops its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries, or an established session continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can sit offline while a separate service processes work it received earlier. So a kill switch works as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools, and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services. When to contain an agent An unexpected action does not by itself mean an agent has suffered compromise. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration, or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context. Signals that warrant a closer look include: * The agent calls a tool or accesses a resource outside its assigned task. * It attempts an unusual volume of reads, writes, or exports. * A workflow continues after an operator believes it has paused. * The agent uses a credential, permission, or integration its owner did not expect. * Identity, application, or network logs show activity that does not match the agent's normal work. The agent's own logs can help explain what it attempted. They remain one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application, and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not prove that the action succeeded. A practical response sequence 1. Pause the affected workflow Stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries, or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided that change does not harm unrelated systems. A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow. 1. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open Source AI Models: 3 Run Paths, 48% Coding Index [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 13, 2026 · 26 min read ![Illustrative: Two technicians in blue vests work at a server rack packed with blue network cables, one holding a tablet](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/open-source-ai-models-3-run-paths-mistral-large-4-kimi-k3-1-glm-5-3-2026-img13-1024x576.webp) Photo: Daoducquan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Five open-weight model families dominate the November 2026 conversation: Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3 and Gemma 4. They share a label and almost nothing else. Mistral publishes a named license (the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT license), while a [third-party comparison of open-weight licenses](https://gpuwerk.com/blog/open-weight-model-licenses/) flags that several rivals need a closer read of the model card before you ship anything on top of them. That gap matters more than a benchmark point. A team that picks the wrong route to a model, whether a vendor API, a hyperscaler catalog or its own GPUs, can end up with a bill, a latency profile or a legal question it did not plan for. Our [self-hosted versus API cost breakdown](https://shattered.io/self-hosted-llm-vs-api-kimi-k3-1-pro-glm-5-3-deepseek-v4-1-mistral-large-4-2026/) covers the hardware arithmetic. The question here is different: for each of the five current open source AI models, which routes exist today, what does each route cost, and what does the official evidence actually confirm? Everything below is dated November 13, 2026. Where an official page confirms a fact, the text says so. Where only a third-party tracker or a forum post supports it, the text says that too, and the table cells stay empty rather than guess. That discipline is the point. The open-model market moves weekly, and a confident but wrong spec costs readers real money. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Open Source AI Models Actually Mean in 2026 Strictly speaking, almost none of these releases are open source in the way the software industry uses the term. The usual bar covers code, data and the freedom to modify and redistribute. What the labs ship is closer to open weights: a downloadable set of parameters, usually with a license that grants some rights and withholds others. Moonshot AI officially calls Kimi K3.1 Pro open-weight, and Mistral calls Large 4 open weight. Neither claims a fully open training pipeline. This comparison uses the phrase open source ai models the way readers do while keeping the distinction visible. When a sentence says open source, read it as weights you can download under some license. When it says open-weight, the lab itself used that word. ### The evidence ladder Not every claim deserves equal trust. We sort the evidence into four rungs and place each model on the ladder: * **Rung 1, official page confirms:** the lab’s own announcement, documentation or pricing page states the fact. * **Rung 2, official page implies:** the lab uses the phrase open-weight or open models without naming a license file. * **Rung 3, third-party tracker:** a pricing or license aggregator reports it, and no official page contradicts it. * **Rung 4, forum or single mention:** a user post or one-off report. Treat it as a lead, not a fact. Mistral Large 4 sits mostly on rung 1. Mistral’s announcement of the open-weight release names the license and its version (v26.10). LLMs.content: [Ai2](/) # XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question November 13, 2026 Ai2 --- [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06842)[Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/XYBench-dataset)[Code](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench) Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing [**XYBench**](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench), a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the *XY problem*: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: *recognizing* when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately *redirecting* them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. ### Building XYBench We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context. For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem. ### Evaluating how an answer helps A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem. A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Comprehensive Scoping Survey Maps Capabilities and Gaps in Autonomous AI Coding Agents ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Comprehensive Scoping Survey Maps Capabilities and Gaps in Autonomous AI Coding Agents](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/stackrss-featured-9753-750x422-bio-b0b40891cdcb-750w.webp) Comprehensive Scoping Survey Maps Capabilities and Gaps in Autonomous AI Coding Agents A comprehensive structured scoping survey published in Data Science and Engineering synthesizes five years of research into artificial intelligence coding agents, charting their shift from simple token completion tools toward systems capable of multi-step repository navigation, tool execution, and iterative defect repair. Conducted by researchers including Yanshu Wang, Chenfeng Yang, Shuyang Hou, Xinye Xu, Bin Cui, Yanbing Jiang, and Tong Yang, the study systematically examines academic literature, tool scaffolds, and commercial ecosystem developments available through February 28, 2026. Rather than claiming exhaustive systematic coverage, the authors characterize their work as a scoping survey grounded in reproducible discovery queries across arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and DBLP, which yielded 18,261 unique deduplicated records before manual qualitative filtering established an analyzed corpus of exactly 154 cited sources. Their central technical conclusion emphasizes that while autonomous coding agents demonstrate verified competencies on curated benchmarks, current architectures exhibit strict boundary constraints, unresolved tool-use failure modes, and highly variable productivity outcomes across practical developer environments. To establish conceptual clarity across an increasingly fragmented field, the survey introduces an analytical five-dimensional taxonomy designed to classify systems without conflating internal computation with supervision policies. The authors organize AI coding systems across interaction paradigm, computational architecture, deployment form, orchestration mode, and human-oversight mode, ensuring that each representative system receives a single primary value per dimension. By treating human oversight as an independent axis rather than an inherent property of computational architecture, the taxonomy resolves earlier classification ambiguities, allowing single-agent systems with strict human approval gates to be distinguished from unconstrained pipelines. The interaction dimension demarcates four operational levels spanning basic token completion, multi-turn conversational coding, bounded multi-step agentic workflows, and speculative lifecycle-wide autonomous targets. The authors emphasize that higher levels of interaction do not indicate empirical maturity, noting that no public evidence establishes reliable end-to-end autonomous software development on production systems. The historical progression documented by the authors traces automated programming from formal program synthesis in the 1960s through statistical code models and search-based automated program repair. The subsequent rise of statistical n-gram models and recurrent neural networks established that source code exhibits natural linguistic regularities, yet these techniques remained confined to short local token sequences. Similarly, first-generation program repair systems such as GenProg revealed that candidate patches frequently satisfied test suites superficially by deleting functionality rather than addressing underlying logical flaws. The survey explains that transformer architectures and large-scale pre-training across vast repositories have fundamentally expanded this design space, allowing models to parse incomplete natural-language requirements, reason across disparate files, and interpret interactive execution feedback. At the private gathering attended by researchers and engineers, Zhang said the company has the capability to compete head-on with OpenAI and Anthropic, but that catching up to frontier technology would take until 2029-2030 at the earliest. A ByteDance spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. The new agent is said to resemble Muse, which Meta unveiled in September. Muse combines voice conversation with animated avatars to handle tasks on users' behalf. It keeps running on cloud virtual machines even after users close the app, sending emails, searching for shopping options and making payments, and asks for user confirmation only at critical steps such as transfers or sends. Meta attracted more than 10 million users in North America within six weeks of launch and is expanding Muse's reach to smart glasses and a dedicated device, the Muse Charm. Behind ByteDance's move to offer a Muse-like service is a strategy to secure early users by linking the agent to its own platforms. With massive traffic from TikTok and Douyin, the plan is to attach the agent to existing services and quickly establish it in the market. ByteDance is said to have run an internal project called Spell since April to integrate personal AI agent capabilities into its mobile assistant Doubao. It has not been confirmed, however, whether the upcoming agent is directly tied to the Spell project. The heaviest emphasis in Zhang's remarks was on data. He lamented that the datasets used by Seed, the company's AI research organization, for large language model (LLM) pretraining are "several orders of magnitude" smaller than those of frontier competitors. The judgment is that with the scaling law still governing model performance, a data gap translates directly into a ceiling on intelligence. Chmielewski and Thomas Buckley Bloomberg A century after Walt Disney Co. transfixed moviegoers with a hand-drawn mouse appearing on a silver screen with synchronized sound, the world’s biggest entertainment company is now exploring a new frontier in animation: artificial intelligence. In December, the company will bring Ozzy Fox, a children’s series rendered by AI, to its flagship Disney+ streaming platform. Ozzy Fox, about an orange character who regularly bursts into song, is the product of a year-long collaboration with French startup Animaj, whose AI tools convert artists’ hand-drawn images and text instructions into three-dimensional animation. It’s just one example of a wider mission, led by Chief Executive Officer Josh D’Amaro, to bring the 103-year-old home of Disney princesses, Pixar and Star Wars into the AI era. Just one week into D’Amaro’s tenure as CEO, OpenAI shuttered its Sora text-to-video platform, scuttling a planned three-year partnership that would have seen Disney invest $1 billion into the startup and license more than 200 of its characters for use in AI-generated short videos. Since then, the company has charted its own course and is leaning on artificial intelligence to upgrade every one of its units from finance to film. At the same time, Disney has been looking to cut costs, moves that have resulted in regular rounds of layoffs as the company’s traditional TV channels struggle to retain viewers and advertisers. D’Amaro’s embrace of AI marks a new approach for Disney. Under former CEO Bob Iger, Disney employed the carrot and the stick. It litigated against startups including Midjourney Inc. and MiniMax over alleged copyright infringement, after images featuring Mickey Mouse brandishing a machine gun or crude depictions of Disney princesses appeared on social media, while collaborating with one, OpenAI, which promised to act responsibly. The false start of Disney’s collapsed deal with OpenAI and the threat of AI replacing artists speaks to Hollywood’s struggle to reconcile the promise of cheaper, faster filmmaking with fears that it could undermine the creative talent and intellectual property on which the industry depends. Those concerns fueled the crippling actors’ and writers’ strikes in 2023 and are simmering throughout an economic downturn in Los Angeles. Few companies have more on the line than Disney. After more than $100 billion worth of acquisitions in the past two decades, from Marvel to Pixar, Star Wars owner Lucasfilm and The Simpsons owner 21st Century Fox, Disney has one of the industry’s richest troves of characters, stories and franchises. Disney hasn’t articulated an overall AI strategy,  but teams across the company are experimenting with different applications, hinting at the potential for broad use of the technology.  In September, the company named  Karandeep Anand - a technology veteran who most recently lead an AI startup - as Disney’s first chief technology officer, in a broad signal of the role AI is likely to play in the entertainment giant’s future. Like other Hollywood studios, Disney began by introducing AI in parts of the business where it is least likely to encounter creative resistance. The company is building Disney Financial Insights - or D-Fi - an AI-enabled collaboration platform that can replace and automate manual budget reports, bringing visibility, approvals and insights into one place, people familiar with the plans said. They share a label and almost nothing else. Mistral publishes a named license (the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT license), while a [third-party comparison of open-weight licenses](https://gpuwerk.com/blog/open-weight-model-licenses/) flags that several rivals need a closer read of the model card before you ship anything on top of them. That gap matters more than a benchmark point. A team that picks the wrong route to a model, whether a vendor API, a hyperscaler catalog or its own GPUs, can end up with a bill, a latency profile or a legal question it did not plan for. Our [self-hosted versus API cost breakdown](https://shattered.io/self-hosted-llm-vs-api-kimi-k3-1-pro-glm-5-3-deepseek-v4-1-mistral-large-4-2026/) covers the hardware arithmetic. The question here is different: for each of the five current open source AI models, which routes exist today, what does each route cost, and what does the official evidence actually confirm? Everything below is dated November 13, 2026. Where an official page confirms a fact, the text says so. Where only a third-party tracker or a forum post supports it, the text says that too, and the table cells stay empty rather than guess. That discipline is the point. The open-model market moves weekly, and a confident but wrong spec costs readers real money. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The usual bar covers code, data and the freedom to modify and redistribute. What the labs ship is closer to open weights: a downloadable set of parameters, usually with a license that grants some rights and withholds others. Moonshot AI officially calls Kimi K3.1 Pro open-weight, and Mistral calls Large 4 open weight. Neither claims a fully open training pipeline. This comparison uses the phrase open source ai models the way readers do while keeping the distinction visible. When a sentence says open source, read it as weights you can download under some license. When it says open-weight, the lab itself used that word. ### The evidence ladder Not every claim deserves equal trust. We sort the evidence into four rungs and place each model on the ladder: * **Rung 1, official page confirms:** the lab’s own announcement, documentation or pricing page states the fact. * **Rung 2, official page implies:** the lab uses the phrase open-weight or open models without naming a license file. * **Rung 3, third-party tracker:** a pricing or license aggregator reports it, and no official page contradicts it. * **Rung 4, forum or single mention:** a user post or one-off report. GitHub’s own materials now treat that description as outdated. On October 28, 2026, the company announced a connected Copilot cloud experience, and the rollout began the same day. TrnRT is an open inference engine for running large language models on Trainium hardware. It combines model execution, caching and an API server in a system designed for teams that compile models on a host and serve them on Trainium. ![The README of the RunanywhereAI/trnrt repository on GitHub](https://news.lavx.hu/api/media/file/runanywhereai-trnrt-readme-2026-11-13.jpg) *Screenshot: the project's README on GitHub* ## What it is TrnRT runs large language model inference on Trainium hardware and serves responses through an API compatible with chat and text-completion clients. The project focuses on the serving path: it includes an inference engine, a request router, caches and a compile pipeline. Its README identifies GLM-5.3-Flash as its first supported model, with support for more open models planned. The project targets teams that want to run model inference on this hardware and connect it to existing client workflows. The engine is built around a model's decode workload, where it generates output after processing a prompt. TrnRT groups the work into kernels designed for Trainium, then routes requests to engines that maintain session state. Its API supports chat and completion requests, streaming responses, tool calls and reasoning output. That combination lets an application use familiar request patterns while TrnRT handles model execution and the hardware-specific serving path. ## How it works TrnRT uses NKI megakernels for decode. Each kernel fuses work across part of a model layer, including attention, mixture-of-experts processing and other model operations. The README says this design keeps working data in on-chip memory, uses the chip's physical cores in a balanced way and places collective operations inside the kernel. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) [tbreak.](/) [Tech](https://tbreak.com/tech/)/[AI](https://tbreak.com/topics/ai/)/[PC](https://tbreak.com/topics/pc/) # llama.cpp reaches version 1.0 for local AI tools The engine behind many local AI setups will flag breaking changes with major-version numbers, so app makers can plan for them. [Tbreak Editor](https://tbreak.com/author/tbreak/) Change language to 0:00 The open-source engine many local AI setups run on, llama.cpp, reached 1.0 on 13 November. Its maintainers now promise app developers that breaking changes will come only with major-version bumps. According to the [ggml-org post on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/llama-cpp-v1), the project has grown a lot in the 3.5 years since it started. The post notes that “many downstream applications already depend on our work.” For an app maker, a breaking change now shows up in the version number, so they can plan for it. > Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount. > > The ggml-org team, Hugging Face blog post ## Subscribe to our Newsletters for more Tech Stories Found us on Google? [Add tbreak as a preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tbreak.com) to see more of our stories in Top Stories. ## What llama.cpp 1.0 actually promises llama.cpp runs AI models; it isn’t a model itself. Two libraries reached v1.0.0 on 13 November 2026: llama.cpp (*libllama*, which handles LLM inference in C/C++) and ggml (*libggml*, the tensor library underneath it). Both now follow semantic versioning, with three kinds of release: * **Major:** a breaking change to the public C API. * **Minor:** a backward-compatible feature, backend update, new model support, or API addition. * **Patch:** a bug fix with no API change. The post says both projects “will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps.” The API is the interface developers use to call the libraries, while the ABI is the binary interface compiled apps rely on. Superpower Daily sums it up as “a signal for downstream teams, not a freeze on change.” ## What changed in the release The 1.0 release also cleared out old code. [Unite.AI’s reading](https://www.unite.ai/llama-cpp-v1-0-0-sets-api-stability-rules-for-local-ai-tools/) of the [GitHub release notes](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/v1.0.0) says it removes the deprecated public API, including 35 deprecated functions. It also moves the NextN speculative-decoding API from llama-ext.h into the public llama.h header. Unite.AI also lists new functionality: * **Memory:** FP8 key-value caches, plus a host-memory cache for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with a configurable CPU share. * **Models:** Kimi-K3.1-Pro, Ripple, xing4\_0 text, drama-3 text-to-speech, and vision for MageVL-Cowork and Kimi-K3.1. * **Server:** fixes for server-side request forgery, CORS, and DNS rebinding; HF\_TOKEN restricted to huggingface.co hosts; and a new OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech endpoint. * **Web interface:** named chat groups and a live-preview Markdown editor. * **Mobile:** layouts that use device safe areas and full-screen dialogues, as well as an Android chat editor that can open the virtual keyboard. Unite.AI says an official llama.cpp release tag is created only when its internal copy of ggml matches the released ggml, so system-wide installs through Debian and Homebrew stay compatible. ## Where it runs The maintainers say ggml “is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence.” It uses dedicated backends that can load at runtime. llama.cpp currently supports more than 150 architecture variants, as well as all mainstream speculative-decoding methods. Pre-release builds cover Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS, with other channels including Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget, and an XCFramework for iOS and macOS. However, its dominance is now being tested following the resignation of its chief executive Jensen Huang, [triggered by revelations of extramarital affairs,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/former-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-had-a-relationship-with-a-second-employee-sources-say?ref=inline-article) including with a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The affair has [intensified scrutiny of Megaspeed where Alice Huang was a former executive.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/who-is-alice-huang-the-chinese-exec-accused-of-spying-on-nvidia-ceo?ref=inline-article) The American authorities have been looking into whether the Singapore-based company aided in bypassing US export controls, specifically examining if chips were being unlawfully rerouted or smuggled into China. These developments in a post-Jensen Huang era may spell trouble for South-east Asia’s AI infrastructure build-out, with experts expecting [data centre operators in the region to face stricter checks on purchases of advanced American chips.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/data-centres-in-se-asia-could-be-the-first-to-feel-heat-from-jensen-huang-affair?ref=inline-article) The Straits Times examines Nvidia’s central role in the AI industry and other viable AI chip alternatives. ## What are Nvidia’s key products? The firm is known for its high-performance compute chips, which power modern tasks such as AI chatbot assistants that can do deep research and code, autonomous vehicles, and delivery robots. Nvidia is traditionally known for designing Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) that deliver optimal graphics for video games and multimedia design. The same technology has grown to become the bedrock of data centres, running massive amounts of calculations simultaneously to train and run AI models. Among its most advanced chips are the Blackwell and Rubin GPUs, which the US authorities have banned from being exported to China, citing security concerns due to the potential for military use. Earlier in September, the chipmaker set foot into the personal computer market with its new RTX Spark Superchip, allowing users to run large AI models and high-end games on laptops. ## How does Nvidia dominate the global market? others are in Shaanxi, Jilin, Inner Mongolia, Gansu, Wuxi and Fujian [[2]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/chinas-3-billionplus-pipeline-of-nvidiapowered-ai-data-centres-5024599). * Reuters said the projects have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Alice Huang, and that it did not establish how the restricted hardware reached Chinese buyers [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). * Hong Kong-listed AI developers fell again on Friday: Z.AI dropped 7.4%, MiniMax 4.9% and Tencent 2.6% in morning trading [[3]](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/asia-stocks-steady-chipmakers-rebound-042520486.html). ![Huang's exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion of Chinese AI data centers built on Nvidia chips, Reuters reports](/media/news_images/huangs-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-of-chinese-ai-data-centers-built-o.jpg) More than $3 billion of Chinese AI data center projects designed around [Nvidia](/companies/nvidia/) processors that the US bars from export to China are at risk of delays, supply disruption or costly redesigns as Washington weighs tighter controls after [Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive](/news/jensen-huang-resigns-as-nvidia-ceo-cfo-colette-kress-named-interim-chief-executive/), Reuters reported on Friday [[1]](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivehuang-exit-and-us-scrutiny-imperil-3-billion-in-chinese-ai-projects-reliant-on-nvidia-5024462). This move is driven by concerns that a scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could lead to tighter US restrictions on remote AI chip access. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Nov 13, 2026 at 11:20 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google") Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google ## Highlights * Chinese AI firms are renting Nvidia-powered computing capacity at overseas data centres. * Concerns over a Jensen Huang scandal could tighten US remote chip access restrictions. * Proposed US Remote Access Security Act (RASA) would regulate cloud access to restricted tech. * Increased demand for Nvidia AI chips in China's grey market fuels stockpiling by traders. Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies are attempting to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres located outside China, according to three people familiar with the matter. This action stems from concerns that a controversy involving [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia)'s chief executive, Jensen Huang, could prompt Washington to tighten restrictions on remote access to advanced processors. US [export controls](/tag/export+controls) currently limit the direct export of Nvidia's most advanced [AI chips](/tag/ai+chips) to China. However, Chinese firms can bypass these restrictions by renting computing power from overseas data centres that utilise such processors. A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally securing overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted data centre operators for reservations. Smaller AI labs are also exploring similar steps, including approaching major providers in Southeast Asia, two of the people said. These companies reportedly fear that the controversy surrounding Huang could add political momentum to the [Remote Access Security Act](/tag/remote+access+security+act) (RASA). This proposed US bill would grant the Commerce Department authority to regulate cloud-based access to restricted technology. The House of Representatives passed RASA in January, and it awaits Senate action. Advanced Nvidia processors are crucial for training and running large AI models that power chatbots and other [generative AI](/tag/generative+ai) products. Restricting overseas cloud access would make it more difficult for Chinese developers to obtain high-end computing power without direct chip imports. ### Market and Enforcement Concerns The prospect of tougher enforcement has also increased demand for restricted Nvidia AI chips in China's grey market. Traders and intermediaries have begun stockpiling these processors, two of the sources stated. Buyers fear the controversy could lead to a broader US crackdown on smuggling advanced chips and AI servers into China. Procurement records indicate that a Chinese university, despite being on a US export blacklist, purchased Nvidia H200 AI chips last month. This highlights existing gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. US prosecutors in March charged Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips to China. This was allegedly done through a Southeast Asia-based company that bought approximately $2.5 billion of servers from Super Micro between 2024 and 2025. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?
